items.title: Modeling the Selective and Lossy Nature of Visual Processing Bridges the Discrepancy in Noninvasive Neural Decoding.
items.abstract: Noninvasive neural decoding seeks to infer visual stimuli from brain recordings, such as EEG and MEG, thereby providing a computational approach for probing human visual information processing. Current contrastive learning approaches align brain signals with image embeddings from pretrained neural networks. However, these methods often struggle with the intrinsic visual-brain discrepancy arising from systematic representational gaps and noise because brain signals are treated as direct, lossless replicas of visual inputs. To alleviate this mismatch, the proposed framework accounts for the selective and information-compressive characteristics of biological vision. On the visual side, the framework incorporates an adaptive, context-aware visual calibration mechanism, where multilevel blurred representations are dynamically fused under the guidance of structural salience to refine visual features toward the brain's abstraction level. On the brain-signal side, a robust and lightweight neural encoder is used to mitigate inter-channel and temporal variations. Experiments on standard EEG and MEG benchmarks show that the proposed method achieves strong brain-to-image retrieval performance. Our modeling hypothesis, supported by retrieval behavior, suggests that computational representations aligning with salient and structurally meaningful content better match macroscopic neural responses than fine-grained image details. These findings suggest that incorporating the lossy and selective characteristics of human visual processing into computational models is important for advancing noninvasive neural decoding and understanding brain-machine alignment. The source codes are available at SLVP.

items.title: A synchronized dual-scale platform combining flexible micro-ECoG and skull-screw EEG reveals frequency-dependent cortex-to-skull spectral gain in awake mice.
items.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is the most scalable window onto brain dynamics, yet how cortical activity is transformed before reaching extracranial electrodes has largely been inferred from forward models rather than directly measured. We built a dual-scale sensing platform in awake mice that records a 16-channel flexible micro-electrocorticography (micro-ECoG) array and five skull-screw EEG electrodes on a single 30-kHz clock, enabling sample-aligned comparison of cortical and skull-level signals. Across 115 simultaneously recorded ECoG-EEG pairs from three mice, cortex-to-skull spectral gain was not frequency-flat but increased with frequency following a power law, indicating that skull EEG relatively preserves high-frequency cortical activity rather than acting as a simple low-pass copy. This gain was also non-stationary: it shifted across blocks of a fixed-order auditory protocol and was not explained by measured video motion, whereas trial-matched cross-scale coherence depended on the reference transform. With channel number equalized, micro-ECoG retained a larger unique spatial component than skull EEG. These results convert the cortex-to-skull relationship from a static modeling assumption into a measurable, frequency- and state-dependent quantity. For neural sensing, they provide an empirical calibration target for choosing electrode scale, reference, and analysis band and for validating EEG forward models and EEG-to-intracranial translation. More broadly, they indicate that noninvasive biomarkers and brain-computer interface features, particularly in high-frequency bands, should be interpreted through frequency- and state-aware cortex-to-skull mappings.

items.title: Enhanced P300-based brain-computer interface decoding via region-weighted multiscale temporal-spatial representation learning method.
items.abstract: P300-based brain-computer interface (BCI) systems provide a vital communication channel for individuals with severe physical disabilities. While deep learning has achieved significant progress in signal processing, P300 recognition remains hindered by low signal-to-noise ratios and non-stationary dynamics. Existing deep learning approaches exhibit two primary limitations: they rely on fixed-scale temporal filters that fail to capture multi-resolution event-related potential (ERP) dynamics, and they treat electrode channels homogeneously, overlooking the functional modularity of cortical regions and the interaction between local and global network patterns. To address the above issue, we propose the Region-Weighted Multiscale Temporal-Spatial Neural Network (RWMTS-Net). The model integrates three key components: a region partition module that groups physiologically aligned electrodes, a multiscale temporal-spatial module that captures multi-resolution ERP dynamics across functional brain regions, and an adaptive channel attention mechanism that dynamically couples local dynamics with global network features. Evaluated on a public dataset and a self-collected dataset under participant-dependent conditions, RWMTS-Net significantly surpassed state-of-the-art baselines (including EEGNet, ShallowNet, EEGInception, PPNN, and DeepNet). It achieved superior average character recognition accuracies of 98.93% and 91.79% on the respective datasets, along with enhanced information transfer rates (ITRs), higher AUC, and lower performance variance. These results demonstrate that RWMTS-Net effectively resolves key spatio-temporal representation bottlenecks, offering a highly accurate and robust solution for BCI decoding.

items.title: A spatio-temporal attention convolutional network with topology-preserving channel embedding and transformer for EEG decoding.
items.abstract: EEG-based BCI has shown promising applications in motor rehabilitation and emotion recognition. Given the non-stationarity and variability of EEG signals, it is essential to develop classification models that can effectively extract spatio-temporal features while maintaining strong generalization capabilities. This paper proposes a spatio-temporal attention convolutional network for EEG decoding (E-STACNet) to encode the topological features and temporal characteristics of EEG signals within a unified network framework. It consists of channel-attention (CA) block, convolutional (CV) layers, multi-head self-attention (MSA) and classifier layer. Specifically, CA block encodes spatial topological feature via a topology-preserving channel embedding method. Then convolutional layers are employed to encode low-level temporal information and further extract spatial features, followed by MSA block to highlight the most important temporal information of EEG signals. Finally, the outputs are obtained through two fully-connected layers. We conducted experiments on three public EEG-based datasets including BCI Competition IV dataset 2a, Giga DB and DEAP. The results demonstrate E-STACNet achieves average accuracies of 88.00% and 80.62% on datasets 2a and Giga DB, respectively. On the DEAP, it reaches average accuracies of 96.49% and 96.46% for valence and arousal. The proposed model outperforms other state-of-the-art models on all three datasets. Additionally, the ablation study reveals the importance of topology-preserving channel embedding for the proposed network. Visualization analysis shows E-STACNet could obtain the importance of channels at different locations through the channel-attention mechanism, which demonstrates the interpretability of the proposed model. Overall, the accurate and generalization capabilities of E-STACNet will promote the development of EEG-based BCIs.

items.title: Emerging promise in artificial vision research: Unveiling transformative potential through brain-computer interfaces.
items.abstract: Brain-computer interface (BCI) technology has driven revolutionary advancements in the field of artificial vision, presenting new opportunities for individuals with visual impairments. This review summarizes the key technological developments, clinical applications, and future challenges of BCI in artificial vision. In the domain of signal acquisition, both invasive techniques (such as MEA, ECoG, and DBS) and non-invasive techniques (including EEG, MEG, fMRI, and fNIRS) have significantly improved signal resolution and stability. Advances in visual encoding have facilitated the more efficient transmission of visual information. Input BCIs, including technologies based on SSVEP and P300, as well as output BCIs involving motor and speech decoding, are progressing rapidly. Clinically, third-generation retinal prostheses (such as Argus II and PRIMA) have helped patients with retinal degenerative diseases regain partial light perception. Based on closed-loop neural feedback, it is expected to help patients with cortical blindness achieve the remodeling of the optic nerve. Nevertheless, technical challenges remain, particularly regarding the long-term stability of neural signals and biocompatibility issues. Emerging solutions such as anti-scarring nanocoatings, self-powered wireless systems, neuromorphic spike encoding, and multimodal sensory integration are addressing several of these challenges. Looking ahead, advancements in neuro-augmented reality are expected to further propel progress in the field. The future of BCI development will depends on continued interdisciplinary collaboration and global cooperation to drive innovation and provide more efficient, accessible visual restoration solutions for patients.

items.title: Exploiting Phase-Sliding Oscillations for Robust Asynchronous Brain-Computer Interface Control.
items.abstract: Asynchronous steady-state visual evoked potential (SSVEP)-based brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) show great potential for real-world control, yet their performance is often impaired by phase shifts between ongoing electroencephalogram (EEG) signals and fixed-phase templates. In this study, we observed and validated a phase-sliding oscillation (PSO) phenomenon: when a fixed-phase template is used, phase-sliding trajectories derived from sliding-window sequences with different initial phases exhibit stable periodic oscillations locked to the stimulus frequency. Based on this finding, we propose a PSO-based asynchronous classification (PSO-AC) method. Specifically, EEG signals are reconstructed into sequences with varying initial phases and transformed into stable time-frequency representations via the wavelet synchrosqueezing transform to extract phase-decoupled features. A probabilistic temporal model is then used to characterize temporal dynamics and distinguish control from noncontrol states. Offline experiments (n = 22) showed that PSO-AC achieved a mean control/noncontrol accuracy of 94.2% with a 2[Formula: see text]s data length, outperforming a state-of-the-art baseline. It also maintained superior performance in nine-class classification under different time delays. In online robotic-arm experiments, PSO-AC enabled more stable command triggering and higher control efficiency, reducing the command cost per successful trial from 4.30 to 1.14.

items.title: Brain-computer interfaces for neurodegenerative diseases: A comprehensive review of closed-loop systems from diagnosis to neural rehabilitation.
items.abstract: Brain-computer interface (BCI) technology serves as an important bridge between the nervous system and external devices and has shown considerable promise for the diagnosis and treatment of neurodegenerative diseases, whose global burden continues to increase: in 2021, more than 57 million people were living with dementia worldwide, with Alzheimer's disease (AD) accounting for approximately 60-70% of cases, while an estimated 11.77 million people were living with Parkinson's disease (PD) in 2021, according to the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021. This growing disease burden, together with the progressive loss of cognitive, motor, and communicative functions, highlights the need for more precise approaches to early detection, functional assistance, and individualized intervention. Conventional diagnostic and therapeutic approaches remain poorly suited to early detection and timely intervention. This paper analyzes the development of BCI technology, from the first detection of electroencephalogram (EEG) signals to the parallel development of invasive and non-invasive systems, and outlines the basic principles of signal acquisition, processing, and decoding, together with the relative advantages and limitations of different approaches. It then focuses on the use of BCI in Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), covering early diagnosis, functional reconstruction, and neuromodulation. The article also discusses the difficulties encountered by BCI technology in terms of technological realization, clinical translation, and ethical considerations, as well as several future research directions, including multimodal fusion, adaptive algorithms, closed-loop control systems, and personalized treatment so as to drive the applications of BCI in precision medicine and in neurological diseases.

items.title: A User-Function Taxonomy for Brain-Computer Interfaces: From Task Definition to Evidence.
items.abstract: Brain-computer interface (BCI) studies are commonly compared by electrode, signal, paradigm, device, or clinical purpose. These descriptors do not identify the user-level function implemented in a task, although that function determines the appropriate endpoint. This article proposes the Type-Wield-Synthesize-Sense (TWSS) framework as a complementary taxonomy. Type involves selecting one option from alternatives specified before a decision. Wield regulates an observable state that remains correctable over time. Synthesize infers intentional expressive content without presenting alternatives at each update. Sense uses neural information to estimate a state for adaptation or therapy, or conveys external information through artificial neural stimulation. The classification unit is a functional episode with stable information direction, task relation, control allocation, and primary endpoint. A purposive, non-systematic literature synthesis and worked analyses of published protocols inform the framework across invasive and noninvasive interfaces. TWSS separates finite choice from inferred expression, discrete command from continuous regulation, and user control from automated assistance. Each class links an application claim to evidence for reliable decisions, safe regulation, faithful authorized expression, valid state estimates, or functionally useful artificial sensation.

items.title: Enhancing Motor Imagery Decoding for Stroke Patients Using Data Augmentation and Transfer Learning.
items.abstract: This study proposes an innovative WalkBCI real-time motor imagery brain-computer interface system to solve the problems of time-consuming model calibration and low EEG decoding accuracy in stroke patients because of individual differences. WalkBCI integrates generative adversarial networks and transfer-learning techniques to generate motor imagery feature data via RM-GAN using the resting data of target subjects, which shortens the time of calibration data acquisition and reduces patient fatigue. Meanwhile, the system enhances classification performance by combining source domain data during transfer learning optimization. The system is evaluated in both offline and online experiments to assess its practicality and stability. The study results show that WalkBCI outperformed traditional methods on the stroke patient dataset. In the offline experiments, the model's accuracy, precision, recall, and F 1-score of the model increased by 3.3%, 2.6%, 3.8%, and 3.4%, respectively. In online experiments, the system maintained stable classification performance with a maximum accuracy of 72.5%, while reducing calibration time by 58%. WalkBCI effectively lowered subjects' fatigue, and the comparison experiments revealed average reductions of 7.5 points in FS-14 scores and 74.05 in frontal theta/beta values. This study offers an efficient and stable solution for real-time EEG decoding, particularly well-suited for motor-imagery tasks in stroke patients.

items.title: Conductive hydrogel bioelectronics for chronic neuromodulation: From biomimetic design and bioactive interfaces to integrated neural platforms.
items.abstract: In biomedical engineering, hydrogel bioelectronics brings together the interface between flexible electronic devices and biological systems, opening up a new way for chronic neural regulation. Here we focus on the recent progress in this field, from material design to system integration. The design of high-performance conductive hydrogels is an entry point. The multi-level structure engineering strategy, such as the introduction of carbon nanotubes or conductive polymers, can raise the conductivity and mechanical toughness together. When biomimetic adhesion molecules such as polydopamine or tannic acid are added, the hydrogel has the ability of wet tissue adhesion, and anti swelling and active anti-inflammatory functions are also embedded in the material system. As a result, the resulting neural interfaces are not only more durable in practical applications but also ensure excellent biocompatibility. Turning to applications. How does this kind of material promote the development of chronic neuromodulation technology? Peripheral nerve repair, brain computer interface, spinal cord injury, autonomic nervous system regulation can be seen in several scenes. The long-term and high-precision recording and regulation of neural signals is exactly the most important link in these applications. Hydrogel electronics does have its own uniqueness in this regard. However, there is still a long way to go between laboratory research and clinical transformation. How to ensure long-term stability? Can controllable degradation be achieved in practice? Will the signal fidelity drop with time? How to optimize wireless operation and system integration? Large scale manufacturing is an unavoidable reality test. These directions are probably the worthy areas for follow-up research. Looking forward, if the lines of intelligent response materials, closed-loop sensing and control, and advanced micro processing technology can be screwed together, hydrogel bioelectronics may truly move towards the next generation of personalized, dynamic and adaptive neural diagnosis and treatment platform.

items.title: ONC201/dordaviprone for H3 K27M-mutant tumors: Discovery, mechanisms, therapeutic potential, and future directions.
items.abstract: ONC201 (dordaviprone) has recently received accelerated approval for the treatment of recurrent H3 K27M-mutant diffuse midline glioma. Originally identified as TRAIL-inducing compound 10 (TIC10), ONC201 is a first-in-class small molecule distinguished by a unique pharmacologic profile. It promotes apoptosis through multiple convergent mechanisms, including upregulation of TRAIL, activation of the integrated stress response (ISR), direct allosteric activation of the mitochondrial protease ClpP, and antagonism of dopamine receptor D2 (DRD2). These pathways converge to engage both extrinsic and intrinsic apoptotic programs, disrupt mitochondrial bioenergetics, and reprogram survival signaling, distinguishing ONC201 from conventional cytotoxic and targeted agents. Preclinical studies have demonstrated broad antitumor efficacy across diverse cancer models. Clinically, ONC201 has progressed rapidly through early-phase trials, establishing a favorable safety and pharmacokinetic profile, with sustained biological activity and weekly oral dosing. Pivotal trials in H3 K27M-mutant diffuse midline glioma demonstrated meaningful clinical benefit, leading to accelerated regulatory approval and making it the first therapy to receive such approval for this devastating disease. Ongoing studies are expanding ONC201's clinical applications to hematologic malignancies and gynecologic cancers, as well as to combination regimens. Despite these advances, emerging resistance mechanisms, including ClpP mutations and adaptive activation of the EGFR and MAPK/AKT pathways, highlight the need for biomarker development and rational combination strategies. Together, these insights position ONC201 as both a therapeutic milestone and a platform for future translational oncology innovation.

items.title: The DDIT4L-TOM40-ATP5A pathway suppresses glioblastoma oncogenesis.
The glioma metabolite, D-2-hydroxyglutarate (D-2-HG), reduces synaptic transmission and epileptiform bursts in neocortical slices.
items.abstract: 80% of patients with low-grade gliomas containing mutations of the metabolic enzyme isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) experience seizures, of which nearly half are drug-refractory. Studies in isolated neuronal cultures have led to the hypothesis that the metabolite of the mutant IDH, D-2-hydroxyglutarate (D-2-HG), is epileptogenic by mimicking glutamate and activating NMDA receptors. To test this hypothesis, we used whole-cell patch-clamp techniques to determine the direct effects of D-2-HG on neuronal and synaptic functions and epileptiform activity in neocortical slices that preserve natural and balanced excitatory-inhibitory neural networks. Acute bath application of D-2-HG (10 mM) for 10-30 min did not cause significant neuronal depolarization, induce epileptiform activity, or alter the input-output relationship in layer V pyramidal neurons. D-2-HG slightly lowered action potential (AP) threshold (∼2-3 mV) and significantly reduced AP amplitude. In neocortical slices with ongoing epileptiform bursts (induced by 0 Mg2+ plus 4-aminopyridine), addition of D-2-HG reduced the frequency of the bursts (prolonged inter-burst intervals) and seizure burden. Moreover, D-2-HG diminished electrically evoked mono- and poly-synaptic excitatory postsynaptic currents. Together, the results demonstrate that short-term exposure to D-2-HG inhibits seizure-like activity in neocortical slices possibly by suppressing excitatory synaptic transmission. Thus, these data do not support the initial hypothesis that D-2-HG may excite neurons and promote seizures by mimicking glutamate actions.

items.title: Transcriptional circuits of the glioma microenvironment: FOSL2 as a master regulator of the pathological niche.
EAAT1 sustains redox homeostasis and temozolomide resistance through glutamate-dependent regulation of the Keap1/Nrf2 axis in glioblastoma.
items.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) exhibits profound metabolic and redox adaptation that supports tumor progression and therapeutic resistance. Here, we identify the glutamate transporter EAAT1 (SLC1A3) as a critical regulator of glutamate-dependent redox homeostasis in GBM. Analysis of TCGA, GTEx, and CGGA datasets showed that EAAT1 expression is elevated in GBM and that higher EAAT1 expression is associated with poor patient survival. Using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated EAAT1 knockout together with biochemical, imaging, transcriptomic, and in vivo approaches, we found that loss of EAAT1 altered extracellular and intracellular glutamate homeostasis, reduced intracellular glutamate, glutamine, and glutathione levels, and increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation. EAAT1 deficiency also suppressed oxidative phosphorylation and ROS-related programs and attenuated the Keap1/Nrf2/HO-1 antioxidant axis, accompanied by reduced GPX4 expression and increased lipid peroxidation. Furthermore, EAAT1 ablation downregulated glutamine synthetase and glutaminase, suggesting impaired glutamine-dependent anaplerotic metabolism. Glutamate supplementation partially restored Keap1/Nrf2/HO-1 pathway protein expression in EAAT1-knockout cells. Functionally, EAAT1 loss inhibited GBM cell proliferation and migration, enhanced sensitivity to oxidative stress and temozolomide (TMZ), and reduced tumor growth in xenograft models. Collectively, our findings establish EAAT1 as a key metabolic regulator linking glutamate transport to antioxidant defense and therapeutic response in GBM. Targeting EAAT1 may therefore represent a metabolic vulnerability for overcoming metabolic and redox adaptation and improving TMZ responsiveness in GBM.

items.title: Repurposing Nelfinavir: AIM2 inflammasome-associated anti-tumor effects in Glioblastoma.
items.journal_full: BIOCHIMICA ET BIOPHYSICA ACTA-MOLECULAR BASIS OF DISEASE
items.journal_abbr: Biochim Biophys Acta Mol Basis Dis
items.abstract: Nelfinavir (NFR), originally developed as an antiretroviral agent for the human immunodeficiency virus, has demonstrated anti-cancer properties across various malignancies; however, its therapeutic potential in Glioblastoma (GBM) remains largely unexplored. In the present study, we investigated the anti-tumor effects of NFR in GBM using a comprehensive panel of experimental models, including established GBM cell lines, GBM cell line-derived spheroids, patient-derived primary glioma cells, and patient-derived glioma organoids. We further evaluated the anti-tumor potential of NFR in combination with standard chemotherapeutic agents, carboplatin and doxorubicin, across these platforms. In vitro analyses revealed that NFR significantly inhibits GBM cell proliferation and induces both apoptotic and necrotic cell death. Additionally, we identified that NFR treatment is associated with activation of the AIM2 inflammasome in GBM cells and may contribute to NFR-induced anti-glioma effects. However, activation of the AIM2 inflammasome alone is not essential to induce its anti-tumor effects in GBM. Collectively, our findings highlight NFR as a promising therapeutic candidate for GBM, exerting its effects through anti-proliferative and pro-death mechanisms.

items.title: Glutamine deprivation elevates EFNB3 and its potential link to macropinocytosis in glioblastoma.
items.journal_full: BIOCHIMICA ET BIOPHYSICA ACTA-MOLECULAR BASIS OF DISEASE
items.journal_abbr: Biochim Biophys Acta Mol Basis Dis
items.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common malignant brain tumor with a poor prognosis and prominent therapeutic resistance. l-glutamine (Gln) is crucial for cancer cell survival, and the microenvironment of GBM is often accompanied by Gln deficiency. To explore the molecular mechanisms by which GBM adapts to Gln deprivation, we performed proteomic profiling of clinical GBM tissues and established a Gln-deprived cell model. Our results showed that EFNB3 was significantly upregulated under Gln deprivation. Our data suggest a potential association between EFNB3 and Rac1-GTP, which may contribute to macropinocytosis through the Cdc42/PAK1 related signaling pathway. Knockdown of EFNB3 suppressed proliferation and macropinocytosis in GBM cells. Notably, the p38 MAPK pathway may correlate with sustained Rac1-GTP abundance and macropinocytosis, whereas blocking p38 MAPK signaling appears to attenuate Rac1-GTP levels and impair macropinocytosis without affecting EFNB3 expression. Collectively, our findings reveal a potential regulatory network involving the p38 MAPK/Rac1-GTP axis linked to EFNB3, indicating that EFNB3 may act as an important modulator of metabolic adaptation in GBM.

items.title: Injection-free, spatially controlled delivery of glioblastoma cells to human brain slice cultures using soft cryogel biomaterials.
items.abstract: Organotypic brain slice culture has emerged as a valuable ex vivo system for studying brain development, function, and disease in a multicellular tissue context. More recently, this has extended to the use of human tissue derived from fetal, post-mortem, or discarded surgical specimens. In glioblastoma research, focal delivery of exogenous cells to brain slices is often technically challenging, particularly when spatial control is required. Here, we present a simple and experimentally accessible method for localized cell delivery to human brain slice cultures using soft donut-shaped cryogel biomaterials. Stereolithography-based 3D printed templates were used to generate well-defined cryogels by sub-zero polymerization of poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate and 3-sulfopropyl acrylate. The resulting macroporous scaffolds were soft, easy to handle, and could be positioned directly on top of human brain slices prior to loading brain tumor cells into the central lumen. This design enabled focal confinement of the administered cells while permitting invasion into the underlying tissue. The ability to tailor cryogel dimensions, together with the straightforward workflow, makes this approach a versatile platform for spatially controlled cell delivery to brain slice cultures. Under the conditions tested, cryogel placement was not associated with an increase in local GFAP (Glial Fibrillary Acidic Protein) signal, supporting compatibility with the tissue during culture.

items.title: Latent knowledge-driven unified representation learning for brain tumor segmentation with missing modalities.
items.abstract: Gliomas are the most common primary malignant brain tumors, characterized by high heterogeneity, diffuse infiltration, and poor prognosis. Accurate tumor segmentation plays a fundamental role in diagnosis, treatment planning, and quantitative analysis. Although multimodal MRI provides rich anatomical and functional information, missing imaging modalities are frequently encountered in real-world clinical practice. Here, we propose a Latent Knowledge-driven Unified Representation Learning (LK-URL) framework for robust glioma segmentation under missing-modality conditions. LK-URL incorporates a Dynamic Adaptive Unified Interaction Module (DAUIM) to model intra- and inter-modality interactions, enabling enhanced tumor-aware feature representation and cross-modal compensation. Furthermore, a Latent Knowledge Collaborative Learning (LKCL) strategy is introduced to transfer structural knowledge from complete to incomplete modality settings via internal full-modality supervision, thereby improving the consistency of feature representations across diverse modality combinations and enhancing segmentation robustness. Extensive experiments on three datasets demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches under missing-modality scenarios, while exhibiting strong generalization ability in real-world clinical settings. The code is available at https://github.com/joey-AI-medical-learning/LK-URL.

items.title: Loss of PIMREG impairs double-strand break signaling and repair.
items.journal_full: BIOCHIMICA ET BIOPHYSICA ACTA-MOLECULAR BASIS OF DISEASE
items.journal_abbr: Biochim Biophys Acta Mol Basis Dis
items.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common primary brain tumor in adults. It is an aggressive type of tumor with an average overall survival of 12-15 months post-diagnosis. Standard treatment involves surgical resection, followed by radiotherapy and chemotherapy with temozolomide (TMZ). However, resistance to treatment is frequently observed. PIMREG is a marker of proliferation highly expressed across different tumor types, with particularly elevated levels in GBM. Our previous study revealed that PIMREG silencing sensitizes GBM cells to TMZ treatment and affects ATM activation, a key apical kinase involved in DNA damage signaling. Given the emerging significance of PIMREG in the DNA damage response, we sought to explore PIMREG's role in DNA damage repair and signaling in GBM cells exposed to genotoxic agents. Here we assessed the functionally enriched pathways associated with high PIMREG expression in GBM patient samples, analyzed the interactome of PIMREG upon treatment of GBM cells with TMZ and evaluated the impact of PIMREG loss on DNA damage signaling, DNA break formation and the repair of double-strand breaks. Our findings reveal that PIMREG functions as a direct substrate for ATM/ATR kinases, interacts with key DNA repair proteins upon TMZ treatment and actively facilitates the cellular response to chemotherapy- and radiotherapy-induced DNA damage. Taken together, PIMREG may function in the DNA damage response, particularly in the signaling and repair of double strand breaks via homologous recombination in GBM cells. In all, our data suggested high PIMREG expression may affect resistance of GBM cells to treatment.
